newsitem.title: UK: London seen losing share of bunker fuel market.
newsitem.headline: London seen losing share of bunker fuel market.

text.p: London's role as a bunker fuel centre may be fading and the focus is likely to shift to the Far East, Middle East and South America, a senior bunker official said on Tuesday.

"It is my own perception that the Far Eastern markets, the South American markets and Middle Eastern markets represent the real future for our industry," said Bob Layton, general manager of Tramp Oil and Marine Ltd.
He pointed to the breakup of traditional oil companies in South America and the emergence of Far East nations.

"London's role in the global bunker market is highly developed and central for most if not all bunker players - can it sustain this position or are other areas of the world about to challenge London's traditional dominance in the bunker industry?" he asked.

Layton said total bunker volume supplied in 1996 within the U.K. was 2.7 million tonnes and the total amount of shipping freight in and out of the U.K. was 550 million tonnes, with almost 50 percent of this freight traffic consisted of liquid bulk traffic from crude oil to chemical-to-oil products.
"We may see less reliance on London and its shipping legal and financial institutions from buyers and sellers as new business opportunities are created," he told a bunker conference.
"It could be argued that there are simply too many brokers, traders working in the London market in an industry that is overplayed."
Leyton said the U.K. bunker market is very fragmented and diverse, divided over many small and medium size ports as opposed to being concentrated in one super port, like Rotterdam or Antwerp.

"Traditionally the U.K. bunker market has lacked the level of competition to stimulate growth and move bunker markets into a position that enables them to compete with the ARA ports and Baltic ports on price.
"There are signs, however, that competition is increasing particularly within the fuel oil sector of the U.K. market," Layton added.

He said fuel oil was a sector in which competition has traditionally been especially lacking, "as each refiner/supplier seems to have stuck to promoting sales in their own territory, resisting or unable to invest in new markets."
